title: One front door for every site: a reverse proxy

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Think of a hotel front desk. Every guest comes through one door, and the desk decides which room they go to. Antoine runs a front desk like that for his websites, using Caddy.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So Caddy is the front desk?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. It's a reverse proxy running in Docker on a small DigitalOcean server, with Cloudflare DNS in front. Visitors hit one address, and Caddy routes each hostname to the right application.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does the server get built?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In two layers. Terraform creates the infrastructure: the server, its cloud firewall, and the Cloudflare DNS records for the main domain and a wildcard. Then Ansible configures everything on the machine.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do those two talk to each other?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Terraform writes its results to a file, and the Ansible playbook reads it. There's even a flag that says Terraform owns the DNS records, so there's one clear owner per record.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what does Ansible set up?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In order: system basics like firewall and fail2ban, a CrowdSec security engine, then the Caddy container itself. Before each new configuration goes in, the current Caddyfile is backed up with a timestamp, and the newest five are kept. Afterwards, Caddy validates the file using the same custom image that runs in production.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Reusable snippets. One writes a rotated JSON log per site. One adds security headers and compression. One returns a quick 404 for scanner favourites like dot env, dot git and WordPress paths, before they ever reach an application.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two. First, several hostnames front static GitHub Pages projects, with a snippet that rewrites paths and headers. Second, Docker normally bypasses the UFW firewall for published ports, so a small systemd unit adds rules in the DOCKER-USER chain to keep only the intended ports open.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What about checking on it afterwards?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A single command downloads the Caddy logs, and a Python script turns the JSON access logs into a PDF report with status codes, latency percentiles and hourly traffic.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Split the job: Terraform for what exists, Ansible for how it's set up, Caddy for who goes where. The full write-up has the deployment diagram.
